summary:
Equatorial Guinea is high risk for trans visitors. The penal code in force since 15 November 2022 does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, and same-sex sexual activity is legal with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation. That absence of an explicit prohibition does not translate into safety on the ground.

Authorities continue to apply the obsolete 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices. A 2020 Draft Law titled 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' would move the conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its current status is unclear. Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT people: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order on 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation.

Detention of LGBT people is documented. A Synergía IHR report on lesbophobia and police raids records police and military intervention in the assembly, expression and residential spaces of lesbian women, and in Bata the collective detention of known lesbians on the stated grounds that 'lesbians are members of a sect', including collective punishment when a single woman is sought.

Public humiliation is used as an enforcement tool. In 2014 four men were detained after a video was found on a phone and were made to explain their actions on national television. A lesbian couple in Añisok were tied up at the police station, paraded through town behind banners calling them witchcraft-practicing lesbians, photographed and shamed. In August 2023 police illegally detained Trifonia Melibea Obono, founder of Somos Parte del Mundo, after her group submitted a report on torture and ill-treatment of LGBTQI+ people to the EU headquarters in Madrid; arrests and restrictions rose significantly afterward. ILGA reports that state intimidation of sexually diverse individuals persists and that LGBTQI+ people are still detained and punished through public shaming despite the lack of an explicit prohibition.

Violence in custody and under state control is reported for trans and gender-nonconforming people. Transgender women have described harassment and sexual violence while in police custody, and security forces have subjected LGBTQI+ people to sexual violence and discrimination in the military, jails and prison. Rape is sometimes used as a form of conversion practice, and queer women are forcibly impregnated in an attempt to make them heterosexual. LGBTQI+ women and transgender men are described as vulnerable to sexual violence in the military and from family members.

Enforcement of protections is weak. Laws against rape are not effectively enforced because the crime is rarely reported, and police and judicial officials may decline to act where the perpetrator has political connections or serves in the police or military. The only provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people is Article 364(2) of the 2022 Penal Code, which bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation; beyond it, the US State Department's 2021 reporting finds no anti-discrimination protections, set within a general context of repression and societal stigma.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and are not eligible to the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples.
tangentialFactors:
The repression of LGBT people sits inside a broader restriction of civic space. A UPR stakeholder submission from Small Media, EG Justice, IPI and Digital Rights in Equatorial Guinea, filed for the country's fourth UN Universal Periodic Review, documents constraints on freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety; the same environment constrains LGBT advocacy and the reporting of incidents.

The August 2023 detention of an LGBTI advocacy founder after a report on torture reached an external audience illustrates how documentation itself carries risk, with arrests and restrictions rising in its wake.

Social climate is described in academic analysis of Trifonia Melibea Obono's 2019 novel 'Yo no quería ser madre', published in Hispanic Studies Review in October 2025, which finds compulsory heterosexuality and queer invisibility in Equatoguinean society.

The criminal code in force is a revision of the Spanish Criminal Code dating to the Francoist era, said to carry anti-homophobic undertones, which helps explain why conduct is not explicitly prohibited while enforcement is nonetheless punitive.
localsOnly:
Residents face discrimination in education and employment. Teachers have reportedly discriminated against and excluded LGBTQ+ girls, and LGBTQ+ children are often forced out of their homes, which frequently causes them to drop out of school. Academics and government employees can be ousted if perceived as not heterosexual.

Article 364(2) of the 2022 Penal Code bars employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, the first provision explicitly protecting lesbian, gay and bisexual people. Law 1/2016 on the Protection of Personal Data, at Articles 10 and 41, protects personal data on 'sexual life' where it entails discrimination.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition and cannot access the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, including in inheritance, hospital visitation and next-of-kin decisions.

Transgender residents have no sourced pathway for changing legal gender markers; the sources reviewed carry no information on legal gender recognition documents.

Transgender children are described by a local NGO as especially vulnerable to commercial sexual exploitation, and minors generally are sexually exploited for commercial sex. School officials have reportedly denied transgender students access to some facilities.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2020 Draft Law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' is unresolved in the sources reviewed; whether it has been tabled, amended or enacted is not stated, and readers should treat it as pending rather than in force.

Entry and visa requirements, border screening practices and any questions posed to travellers about gender identity or HIV status are not sourced in this inventory, so no finding is recorded on whether arrival procedures risk outing a visitor.

No sourced information was found on legal gender recognition documents, medication, hormone access or health services, on bathroom or facility access for visitors, or on hate-crime sentencing enhancements. Absence of sourcing is not evidence of absence.

The IRB-CISR country information entry returned no usable finding on Equatorial Guinea in this pass, so the refugee-risk assessment of that body is unrepresented here.

US State Department reporting dates from 2021 and predates the 2022 Penal Code; its statement that no anti-discrimination protections exist has not been re-verified against later editions for this record.
